input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-510: Introduction to Computer Graphics. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Introduction to Computer Graphics is a study of the hardware and software principles of interactive raster graphics. Topics include an introduction to the basic concepts, 2-D and 3-D modeling and transformations, viewing transformations, projections, rendering techniques, graphical software packages and graphics systems. The course will focus on rasterization techniques and emphasize the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders. Students will use a standard computer graphics API to reinforce concepts and study fundamental computer graphics algorithms. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: MATH-241 and (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-610. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[khronos-opengl]
The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.

[mit-computer-graphics]
Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.

[rit-csci-510]
Introduction to Computer Graphics is a study of the hardware and software principles of interactive raster graphics. Topics include an introduction to the basic concepts, 2-D and 3-D modeling and transformations, viewing transformations, projections, rendering techniques, graphical software packages and graphics systems. The course will focus on rasterization techniques and emphasize the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders. Students will use a standard computer graphics API to reinforce concepts and study fundamental computer graphics algorithms. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: MATH-241 and (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-610. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages before rasterization.
beats.example: A vertex shader modifies position and color attributes for each triangle vertex before they reach the rasterizer.
beats.title: Pipeline Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal flowchart with labeled stages: Vertex Shader -> Geometry Shader -> Rasterizer -> Fragment Shader -> Framebuffer.

beats.claim: Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles for downstream processing.
beats.example: Three connected vertices form a triangle primitive that the rasterizer will convert into a set of pixel candidates.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly
beats.visualDirection: Show a wireframe triangle with vertices labeled A, B, and C, highlighting the edges connecting them.

beats.claim: Clipping removes portions of primitives that fall outside the view volume before rasterization.
beats.example: A large triangle extending beyond the camera's field of view is clipped to fit within the viewport boundaries.
beats.title: Clipping Process
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a triangle partially outside a rectangular viewport, with the clipped portion shaded in gray and the visible portion in white.

beats.claim: Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates on a discrete pixel grid.
beats.example: Each pixel within the clipped triangle receives a set of interpolated vertex attributes for processing.
beats.title: Rasterization Conversion
beats.visualDirection: Render a grid of pixels covering a triangle, with each pixel showing a small coordinate index and a dot representing the fragment candidate.

beats.claim: Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs using linear or perspective-correct methods.
beats.example: Color and texture coordinates are calculated for each pixel based on the weighted average of the triangle's vertex attributes.
beats.title: Interpolation Mechanism
beats.visualDirection: Draw a triangle with gradient shading across its surface, showing how values transition smoothly from vertex to vertex.

beats.claim: Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations using shader programs.
beats.example: A fragment shader applies a lighting model to each pixel, calculating final color based on material properties and light direction.
beats.title: Fragment Processing
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a wireframe triangle and a fully shaded triangle with computed colors.

beats.claim: Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values to handle overlapping geometry.
beats.example: A closer triangle overwrites a farther triangle's pixels because its depth values are smaller than the stored depth buffer.
beats.title: Depth Testing & Visibility
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate two overlapping triangles with depth values displayed as numerical annotations, showing the closer one winning the test.

beats.claim: Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value to achieve transparency effects.
beats.example: A semi-transparent overlay triangle mixes its computed color with the background color using a specified alpha factor.
beats.title: Blending Operations
beats.visualDirection: Display a background rectangle and a semi-transparent triangle on top, with a formula showing alpha blending calculation.

beats.claim: Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit to maintain visual correctness.
beats.example: Vertices are transformed from model space to clip space using a projection matrix before being converted to normalized device coordinates.
beats.title: Coordinate Spaces & Projections
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of three nested coordinate spaces (model, view, clip) with arrows indicating transformation flow.

beats.claim: Durable concepts and problem-solving methods are reinforced by verifying pipeline stages, transformation accuracy, and rendering parameters.
beats.example: Instructors verify that vertex attributes are correctly interpolated, depth buffers are updated, and blending modes match intended visual outcomes.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a checklist with checkboxes for: 1. Shader stage execution order, 2. Coordinate transformation accuracy, 3. Depth and blending parameter validation.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of the hardware rasterization pipeline and explain their sequential processing of geometric primitives.
Apply coordinate transformations and projection matrices to map 3-D scene geometry into a 2-D image plane for rendering.
Evaluate the impact of rasterization parameters, such as depth testing and blending, on visual correctness and performance in interactive graphics.
